voiceover.text: Last time, we saw that chlorine pulls hard on its outer electrons, and sodium holds its outer electron loosely. Chemists measure that grip in two different ways. One asks how much energy it takes to pull an electron right off an atom. The other asks how strongly an atom pulls on electrons it shares with another atom. These are first ionisation energy and electronegativity. Let's see how both follow the structure of the atom.

First ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from each atom in a mole of gaseous atoms. A mole is a fixed, very large number of atoms. Gaseous just means the atoms are separate, with nothing else attached. For sodium, each atom loses one electron and becomes a sodium ion. That takes four hundred and ninety-six kilojoules for a mole of sodium atoms. It's called first, because it removes only the first, most loosely held electron.

Now go across Period three. From sodium to argon, the first ionisation energy generally rises, from four hundred and ninety-six, to fifteen hundred and twenty-one kilojoules per mole. That's the same cause as last time. The core charge climbs while the electrons stay in the same shell, so the atoms get smaller, and the outer electrons are held more tightly. It takes more energy to pull one off. Removing chlorine's outer electron takes about two and a half times the energy needed for sodium's.

But look closely. The rise isn't perfectly smooth. Aluminium is lower than magnesium. Aluminium's outer electron is the first one in a three p subshell, which is higher in energy than magnesium's three s, so it's easier to remove. And sulfur is slightly lower than phosphorus. Sulfur's fourth three p electron has to share an orbital with another electron. The two repel each other, so one of them is easier to remove. Exam answers say first ionisation energy generally increases across a period.
Quick prediction. Lithium is at the top of Group one, and caesium is near the bottom. Caesium has fifty-two more protons. Which one needs more energy to lose its outer electron? Have a think.

scenes.title: down a group: further out, easier to remove

voiceover.text: Lithium. Going down Group one, each element has an extra occupied shell, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus. The core charge stays at plus one, so the extra protons don't help. Further away means a weaker attraction, so less energy removes the electron. First ionisation energy falls from five hundred and twenty for lithium, to three hundred and seventy-six for caesium.

Now the second measure. In a covalent bond, two atoms share a pair of electrons. Electronegativity is how strongly an atom in a bond attracts that shared pair. Think of a tug of war, with the shared pair as the rope. The atom with the stronger pull draws the pair toward itself. Electronegativity has no units. It's a scale, called the Pauling scale, and fluorine is the strongest, at four point zero.

Electronegativity follows the same atomic structure. Across Period three, the core charge rises and the atoms shrink, so the pull on a shared pair gets stronger, from zero point nine for sodium to three point two for chlorine. Down Group seventeen, each extra shell puts the shared pair further from the nucleus, so the pull weakens, from four point zero for fluorine to two point seven for iodine. So the most electronegative elements sit at the top right of the table, and the least at the bottom left.

So both measures rise across a period and fall down a group, but they're not the same thing. Ionisation energy is an energy, for one separate atom losing an electron. Electronegativity is a number on a scale, for an atom in a bond pulling on a shared pair. The noble gases show the difference. Argon has the highest first ionisation energy in Period three. But noble gases almost never form bonds, so they usually have no electronegativity value at all. That doesn't mean zero. It means there's nothing to measure.
So here's a picture to keep. Top right holds tight, bottom left lets go.

Your turn. The first ionisation energy of sodium is four hundred and ninety-six kilojoules per mole, and for potassium it's four hundred and nineteen. Explain this difference in terms of atomic structure. Pause here to answer.

Potassium has one more occupied shell, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus. The core charge is plus one for both, so the extra protons are balanced by extra inner electrons. A weaker attraction means less energy is needed to remove it. Saying potassium has more protons, so it holds tighter, is the classic slip. Distance and shielding win.

Last one. Look across Period three, from sodium to argon. Which element has the highest first ionisation energy, and which has the highest electronegativity? Explain why the answers are different. Pause here to answer.

Argon has the highest first ionisation energy, at fifteen hundred and twenty-one. Chlorine has the highest electronegativity, at three point two. They differ because electronegativity describes an atom in a bond, and argon almost never forms bonds, so it has no value. First ionisation energy can be measured for any separate atom. Answering argon for both is the trap.
